title: Historical automation: Occupational loss differs from unemployment
desc: Distinguishes incumbent harm, occupational standing and cohort employment, with robustness checks unable to remove generalization limits.

kps.k: Historical automation evidence distinguishes occupational displacement from cohort-wide employment loss—and both from harm to incumbent workers.
kps.d: Answering the Call of Automation finds that mechanizing telephone operation reduced operator employment among successive cohorts of white, American-born women aged 16–25 by 0.66 percentage points, against a reported mean of 1.15%, while the overall working share changed by an insignificant 0.03 points. In a separate matched-worker analysis, incumbent operators were 3.6–4.2 points less likely to work a decade later; losses reached 6.6–7.5 points among those initially aged 26 or older. These findings describe adjustment alongside concentrated losses, not competing conclusions about the same population. The practical implication is to track displaced workers separately from subsequent entrants rather than infer individual recovery from stable cohort employment.

qs.q: Notes: Table reports effect of cutovers on decade-later outcomes of women who reported being telephone operators in the telephone industry in a given census year, as a function of whether their city had its first cutover in the intervening decade, relative to a matched control group.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Employment adjustment did not necessarily preserve occupational standing.
kps.d: Among working women aged 16–25, the telephone study estimates a 1.51-point decline in operator employment alongside increases of 0.52 points in typing and secretarial work and 0.81 points in waitressing. Average log occupation scores fell by 0.010, with declines concentrated among younger women. Incumbent operators who remained employed experienced a larger 0.056 decline in log occupation score and roughly a 10-point increase in the probability of dropping an occupation-score decile. Occupational scores describe job composition, not directly measured individual wage losses; nevertheless, they qualify any interpretation of unchanged employment as costless adjustment.

qs.q: The other occupations across columns are: (i) office machine operators, (ii) typists, stenographers, and secretaries, (iii) other office clerks, (iv) sales clerks, (v) beauty parlor workers, and (vi) restaurant workers.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The evidence leaves the mechanism of job absorption partly unresolved.
kps.d: The telephone study considers whether expanding demand absorbed would-be operators or whether additional labor supply pushed workers into existing jobs at lower wages. Its 1939 wage comparisons provide little evidence of broad wage compression, but their interpretation depends on labor-market segmentation by age or sex. The sex-based table contains marginally significant negative office-machine and positive waitressing estimates, qualifying the prose’s broader null characterization. Nor does rapid national growth in drug-store waitressing establish an automation-induced demand response: the authors find no cutover effect on employment in that segment. The supplied material therefore presents alternative explanations rather than a demonstrated general mechanism of job creation.

qs.q: 54 ^LE     Adjustment Mechanisms E.1     Shifts in labor supply  A potential explanation for our finding that future cohorts’ found work in other occupations after telephone operation was mechanized could be that rather than demand shifting out to accommodate these workers, demand held steady, supply shifted out, and equilibrium wages fell.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: We find no differential gaps in   younger versus older white, American-born women’s weekly wages (in 1939) in cities which   have versus have not had their first cutover by 1940.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Robustness checks support the main employment pattern without eliminating identification and generalizability limits.
kps.d: The telephone study uses staggered difference-in-differences and event studies in smaller cities, where dial conversion typically occurred as a single event. Expected-employment-growth controls leave the main estimates largely unchanged, addressing the concern that anticipated demand growth induced automation and concealed losses. However, telephone operation and possibly secretarial work showed differential pretrends, and decade-specific tests have limited power. Large-city estimates using 1920–1940 changes and adoption intensity reproduce operator declines without detectable overall employment losses, but also show lower schooling. Null estimates do not establish zero harm, and findings for this historical population do not predict contemporary AI’s effects on legal employment.

qs.q: The evidence indicates that most outcomes were not changing differentially (over the prior 10 years) in cities with an impending cutover, with the exception of employment in telephone operation, which was growing prior to cutovers, and possibly employment in secretarial work, which we show in the paper absorbed many of the women who might have otherwise been operators.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Although these comparisons are potentially somewhat underpowered, the baseline parameter (first row) is near zero, and the interactions with cutover decade (second and third rows) are still within confidence intervals, even using Table VII’s standard errors.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The occupational-task excerpt adds a measurement perspective, not independent evidence of a particular displacement pattern.
kps.d: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change reports separate OLS regressions across 470 consistently coded occupations, measuring task changes between the 1977 and 1991 Dictionary of Occupational Titles revisions in centiles of the 1984 distribution. Missing column headings prevent attribution of numerical coefficients to particular tasks. This material distinguishes task-level measurement from worker and employment outcomes, but cannot substantiate claims about which skills technology displaced or complemented, or corroborate the telephone study’s adjustment findings.

qs.q: Each column presents a separate OLS regression of ten times the annual change in the occupational task measure (measured in centiles of the 1984 distribution) between the 1977 and 1991 DOT revisions.
qs.a: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration · Academia · 2003

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research sources support the proposition that occupational displacement, cohort-wide employment loss and harm to incumbent workers are distinct outcomes. The telephone-automation study provides the direct evidence: mechanization substantially reduced telephone-operator employment among successive cohorts without a detectable reduction in their overall employment, while a separate matched-worker analysis found persistent employment losses among incumbent operators, especially older incumbents. It also shows that continued employment could involve occupational downgrading, so stable aggregate or cohort employment should not be interpreted as costless adjustment. Material internal variation concerns evidentiary scope rather than disagreement. The occupational-task study measures changes across occupations but supplies no worker-level or employment outcomes, so its position on the principal proposition is unclear; it contributes only a distinction between task measurement and labour-market outcomes. The telephone study itself retains uncertainty about absorption mechanisms, pretrends, statistical power and generalisability to contemporary technologies and populations. These findings characterize this curated selection of research sources, not academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The pre-2015 source contributes a measurement distinction consistent with the proposition’s caution against conflating occupational change with employment outcomes: it analyses changes in occupation-level task measures across 470 consistently coded occupations. However, it provides no worker-level, cohort-employment or incumbent-outcome evidence with which to assess the proposition’s principal claim that occupational displacement differs from unemployment and from harm to incumbent workers. Missing table headings further prevent substantive interpretation of which tasks changed. It therefore supplies methodological context rather than independent support for—or opposition to—the proposition.

qs.q: Each column presents a separate OLS regression of ten times the annual change in the occupational task measure (measured in centiles of the 1984 distribution) between the 1977 and 1991 DOT revisions.
qs.a: The Skill Content of Recent Technological Change: An Empirical Exploration · Academia · 2003

elens.an: Within this curated period-specific evidence, the source supports the proposition that occupational displacement, cohort-wide employment effects and incumbent-worker harm must be analysed separately. Its telephone-automation estimates pair a sharp reduction in operator employment with no detectable decline in overall employment among successive cohorts of young women, while the separate matched-worker analysis finds persistent employment losses for incumbent operators, especially older incumbents. The source also supports the proposition’s qualification that stable cohort employment was not costless: workers reallocated into other occupations, occupational standing declined, and incumbents who remained employed experienced occupational downgrading. Material internal variation concerns outcomes and evidential limits rather than the central direction: younger cohorts adjusted more successfully than existing operators; large-city results included lower schooling; wage evidence did not establish the mechanism of absorption; and pretrends, statistical power and design assumptions constrain causal interpretation. Because the study examines historical telephone mechanisation rather than contemporary generative AI, it supports the cluster’s historical distinction but does not establish that the same employment pattern will follow from the 2023–2024 generative shock.
